newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission to debate gene-modified food policy.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission to debate gene-modified food policy.

text.p: The European Commission, aware of consumer unease in the wake of the mad-cow-disease beef scare in Europe, pledged on Wednesday to review EU procedures for clearing gene-modified products.
Commission President Jacques Santer made the pledge during the EU executive's weekly meeting after talks on approval procedures for Ciba Geigy's gene-modified maize.

"The president at the end of the debate over maize underlined that, as shown by the other public discussion over soybeans, genetically modified products pose a problem with public opinion," said spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas.

The EU has already approved several gene-modified products for sale in the 15-country bloc, including U.S. chemical company Monsanto's Round Up Ready soybeans, which have been altered to resist one of the company's weedkillers.

Recent U.S.-origin shipments of soybeans, thought to contain some gene-modified beans from this year's harvest, have sparked direct-action protests by environmentalists and verbal complaints from European consumer organisations and retailers who want to be able to tell customers which products contain derivatives from gene-modified beans.

European Union approval for Swiss company Ciba's gene-modified corn has been held up repeatedly amid concerns about its safety, with many of the EU's environment ministers saying they were against approval at a meeting last June.

"To prevent such a problem arising each time, we are going to start at zero. The president has concluded that the Commission should soon have an orientation debate to see how the problem that now exists can be resolved," van der Pas told a news conference.

European consumer distrust, both about food safety and the authority of food scientists' recommendations, has grown this year in the wake of findings showing a possible link between Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy, the fatal brain-wasting disease in cattle, and its human equivalent in people who have eaten infected beef.
